Q: Approximately locate an image within another A:

Template matching is a technique for finding similar images within larger images, but it requires the template to be of the same size as in the sub-image. In this example OpenCV was used, but it can also be done using scikit-image.

import cv2
from imageio import imread

img = imread("https://i.sstatic.net/OIsWn.png", pilmode="L") 
template = imread("https://i.sstatic.net/fkNeW.png", pilmode="L")

# threshold images for equal colours
img = cv2.threshold(img, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)[1]
template = cv2.threshold(template, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)[1]

aspect_ratio = template.shape[1] / template.shape[0]

# estimate the width and compute the height based on the aspect ratio
w = 380
h = int(w / aspect_ratio)

# resize the template to match the sub-image as best as possible
template = cv2.resize(template, (w, h))

result = cv2.matchTemplate(img, template, cv2.TM_CCOEFF)
min_val, max_val, min_loc, max_loc = cv2.minMaxLoc(result)

top_left = max_loc
bottom_right = (top_left[0] + w, top_left[1] + h)

cv2.rectangle(img, top_left, bottom_right, 127, 3)

cv2.imwrite("europe_bounding_box.png", img)

Result:

Although this example uses a predetermined estimated width, it is also possible to test a range of possible widths and determine which value results in the best match.

Q: Receiving error: AttributeError: module 'cv2.cv2' has no attribute 'CompareHist' when trying to call a openCV method A:

Try using cv.HISTCMP_CORREL instead of CV_COMP_CORREL in the CompareHist method like cv.CompareHist(des1[0], des2[0], CV_HISTCMP_CORREL). It was renamed in the newer versions.

Refer to this post for more information.

Q: Does a BigQuery subquery partition filter (`WHERE dt = (SELECT MAX(dt) FROM t)`) ever prune at runtime? A:

Yes — BigQuery does prune partitions at runtime for certain subquery filter forms, but it's undocumented, cost-based, and gated by table size. The dry-run estimate never reflects it; only actual `total_bytes_billed` reveals it.

Results:

Five date/timestamp-partitioned tables, ordered by size. Numbers are actual GB billed; ✅ = pruned to the latest partition, ❌ = full scan. Tested in `europe-west1`, August 2026.

| Table | Partitioning | Partitions | Size | literal | scalar `=` | `IN` / `JOIN` | `QUALIFY` |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| A | monthly | 27 | 0.42 GB | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

| B | monthly | 40 | 1.95 GB | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |

| C | monthly | 149 | 18.9 GB | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |

| D | daily | 1,324 | 61 GB | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |

| E | daily | 1,297 | 98.8 GB | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |

Example absolute numbers for Table C (18.9 GB): full scan and `QUALIFY` = 18.9 GB billed; scalar `=` / `IN` / `JOIN` = 0.82 GB billed; literal = 0.01 GB billed.

Query used to check billed bytes:

SELECT job_id, total_bytes_billed, query
FROM `region-europe-west1`.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS_BY_USER
WHERE creation_time > TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 15 MINUTE)
ORDER BY creation_time DESC;

## How it works (two stages)

**1. Plan-time (static) pruning** — eliminates partitions from predicates whose value is known before execution (literals, `CURRENT_DATE()`, etc.). This is what the docs describe and what the dry-run reflects. Subqueries never qualify here.

**2. Runtime (dynamic) pruning** — during execution BigQuery evaluates the subquery and pushes the result as a dynamic filter into the partition scan. This is undocumented, shows up only in billed bytes, and appears to be a cost-based / best-effort decision:

- A scalar `=` subquery gets pushed into the partition scan at a lower cost threshold (~2 GB in this sample).

- `IN` / `JOIN` go through a hash semi-join whose partition pushdown only kicks in for larger tables (~19 GB in this sample).

- `QUALIFY dt = MAX(dt) OVER ()` — the window function never prunes at any size tested.

- A literal always prunes plan-time and is the only form whose saving shows up in the dry-run estimate.

Size and partition count rose together in this sample, so I can't fully separate "bytes scanned" from "partition count" as the trigger. The pattern is consistent with a full-scan-cost threshold: pruning is only applied when the scan it avoids is expensive enough to justify the overhead.

## Why the scalar `=` still costs more than a literal

For WHERE dt = (SELECT MAX(dt) FROM t), the bill is:

\> cost of scanning the partition column to compute `MAX(dt)` across all partitions

\> + cost of the pruned outer scan of one partition

The literal skips the `MAX()` scan entirely, which is why it's dramatically cheaper (0.01 GB vs 0.82 GB for Table C). That `MAX()` floor grows with partition/row count.

A CTE vs a nested subquery makes no difference — BigQuery inlines CTEs. What matters is the operator: `=`, `IN`, or `JOIN`.

## Practical takeaways

- Default to WHERE dt = (SELECT MAX(dt) FROM t) for "latest partition." It prunes across the widest range of table sizes with plain SQL. On a very small table it may full-scan, but that scan is cheap anyway.

- Use a literal (or inject one at pipeline build time) when you need pruning *guaranteed* regardless of table size — e.g., when using `maximum_bytes_billed` guardrails or dry-run cost checks.

- Don't rely on `IN` / `JOIN` to prune on small-to-medium tables; they only prune reliably on large ones.

- Avoid `QUALIFY MAX() OVER ()` as a partition filter — it always full-scans. It's fine for picking rows *within* an already-pruned result set.

- Always verify with actual billed bytes, not the dry-run estimate, and use `SELECT *` (or a wide projection) — see the caveat below.

## Don't benchmark with `SELECT <partition column>` only

If you project only the partition column, the `MAX()` subquery's scan of that column equals the full single-column scan of the pruned query, so both report the same bytes and you'll wrongly conclude pruning isn't happening. Use `SELECT *` or a wide projection so the pruned outer scan is visibly smaller than the full scan.

---

Runtime dynamic pruning is undocumented and not a guarantee; measured in `europe-west1`. Re-verify with billed bytes on your own tables and region before depending on it._

Q: why can't i read any video with openCV 3 and python2.7? A:

It is because your code didn't find that video. Either make sure your video is in the same directory as your source code or give it an absolute path.

For working with paths, its better to use a dedicated module which can handle path modifications for you, like https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html.
